en: I know the ways of the Kyrgyz;
Patterned chests, ten carpets,
I know the ways of the Ogoy.
If you ask about our people,
They have more rice than common grain,
More silver than tin,
More foxes than gray hares.
If you ask about our people,
Their treasures and possessions are countless.
Playing shabiyet, making merry,
There is much laughter among our people.
Adorned hips and broad braid ornaments,
Our land has beautiful young wives;
Red dresses, slender waists,
Our land has beautiful maidens.
Argyn and Kyrgyz together,
Our people dwell mingled;
Kumys by day, girls by night,
Such is life among our people!
Those are our people's ways.
My precious son, listen;
Now I shall tell you how things were.
Do not dig my pit;
Do not stir up my misery,
Do not keep bringing down upon me,
My son, suffering no human should inflict!
My plump, gray-mottled goshawk,
My gray hawk, my morning star,
You whom I saw at death's door,
My mirror, left by my khan!
Looking at you, my belly is full;
I have no one besides you.
So many days remain for me to see;
Whom have I besides you?
My hoof left by the winged steed,
My young, unspent warhorse,
My banner fastened to a spear,
Semetey, my gift left by the Magnanimous.
You whom I kiss with parted lips,
You whom I see with open eyes,
I shall tell the truth of these words;
Listen here, my solace.
When your father died,
When this wretched soul suffered,
My Magnanimous One's countless riches,
When all the scoundrels divided them,
I wished to die for my honor;
I did not die, Semetey,
Because you, orphan, were there.
I wished to depart for my honor;
I did not depart, my foal,
Semetey, because you were there.
The dear bird called the wild duck
Flies without turning back for food.
How much I endured, my foal,
For you alone, Semetey!
The wretched bird called the kite
Swoops down in flight for food.
I suffered much humiliation from the scoundrels,
My foal, my child, for you!
Weeping aloud, for your sake,
I came wandering without dying,
Entirely for your sake.
The butchery of the six scoundrels?
Then there also passed over me
The torment of your grandfather, that swine of a khan!
The six babbling fools
Raided my caravan in Keng-Kol;
I came grieving and wandering,
Wandering, unable to avenge myself on the six scoundrels!
Afflicting and beating my suffering,
Ruining my Sart in Keng-Kol,
A curse upon womanhood!
I could not avenge myself on the scoundrels.”
Hearing this, the boy grew excited,
Unable to restrain his agitation.
His poor heart was torn,
His ribs seemed to come apart,
His might appeared before the people.
He raged without restraint.
Hearing the formidable bald man's words,
Hearing that his homeland lay elsewhere,
‘The fine lad has another name,’
‘His father is someone quite different,’
Hearing the bald woodcutter's words,
That his father was the fierce Khan Manas,
That he was born surpassing others,
Hearing his mother's words,
Hearing that his people were Kyrgyz,
The orphan could not restrain his excitement.
His eyes blazed like a lion's;
His mighty teeth, broad as doors,
He ground hard, again and again.
Unrestrained, his thoughts were torn;
Flames poured from his mouth.
‘My father, Khan Manas, do not die!’ he said.
His grief was plain to see.
‘Can a lord's offspring prosper
While wandering in exile?
Can one who has not reached his renowned people
Be a Muslim in faith?
Can a khan's only child
Have gone wandering astray?
Unable to reach a people who would shelter him,
Could anyone be as wretched as I?
Who followed twelve spiritual masters,
My valiant father, stay alive!
Wandering and straying in Bukhara,
Wretched head, never become a man!
Where is the strength I relied upon?
My inheritance left by my valiant father,
Where are the renowned Kyrgyz people?
Turning toward the Kyrgyz, toward Talas,
Will there be a day for this valiant soul to go?’
Back then Kanykey came in mourning,
Semetey came an orphan,
Plundering my goods and prospering,
Semetey came to Bukhara and grew up.
All his world was in harmony;
He became a lion like his father.
Hearing his mother's words,
Only now he heard that dear,
Fierce Manas was his father.
Seeking shelter in its narrow streets,
Through twelve-gated Bukhara
The orphan wandered in a frenzy.
Dust rose from his steps.
In the city of Bukhara,
Unable to contain his strength,
When they saw your boy,
The people were scared out of their lives.
The excited boy took the direct way,
To Manas who had gone to the other world,
To go and recite the Quran.
‘A white beast left by the noble one,’ he said,
Leading Taytoru, the boy went.
As the excited boy was leaving,
His maternal grandmother Altynay,
Shrieking and weeping in distress,
Then went in earnest
To plead with Khan Temir:
“My dear Khan Temir,
You were a hard-hearted khan,
You were a man stingy with livestock!
If you do not agree
To what this orphan here says,
If you do not give him
This Aktulpar here as a gift,
If, offended, he goes to Bukhara,
He will plunder my possessions,
He will wreak havoc altogether.
He will utterly destroy us;
The wretched city of Bukhara,
He will slaughter it all!
Let the boy not cause an uproar,
Beat all the girls,
And drive them away to Talas.
If you offend this orphan,
Let him not make a spectacle.
He grew up an orphan,
And so joined the ranks of men;
He came to Bukhara and prospered,
He came troubled and became mighty.
It was a coat no bullet pierced:
Dress him in the blue padded coat.
It was a steed no bullet reached:
Mount him on Aktulpar.
Let no resentment remain within him;
Show him your fatherly care!
If his fury seizes him,
Let him not devour Bukhara's people,
Let him not say, ‘He is a wicked man,
My maternal grandfather has turned wicked.’
Take heed of what I say:
When slung, the mirror of one's shoulder,
When wielded against a clashing enemy,
The comfort of a life held in trust,
Ochogor when at play,
Koychagyr when in earnest,
Almabash, the finest iron,
Which makes no distinction between far and near,
When a life held in trust is hard pressed,
Does not fail for twelve days.
My khan, agree to what I say;
To your daughter's son who has sheltered in Bukhara,
Give the gray short gun!”
His grandmother cried out,
“Give the property as a gift!”
She kept saying through her sobs.
As soon as Khan Temir heard,
Surrounded by a garden of plane trees,
With a golden throne in the middle,
Though soaked in water forty years,
Not the slightest edge had faded;
Though soaked in water eight years,
It had not frayed or rotted.
From upon the golden throne,
From the surface of that carpet,
He ran in haste.
A tower stood at the foot of the throne;
He ran to the tower,
Climbed up and looked:
That orphan Semetey
Had put on the guise of Manas.
His wrath terrified souls;
A black-spotted leopard
Raged at his side.
A short-tailed, fierce lion
Stood ready beside him.
A banner fluttered in his hand;
The gray pouch-belt left by his father Manas
Gleamed about his mighty waist.
A cap of gray lynx and marten
He had put on his head, excited.
Royal Bukhara's city,
As though he would slaughter it all,
The boy stood in a frenzy.
The keen steel left by his father Manas
He had slung snugly upon his forearm.
The battle-axe with golden cheeks
He had taken from his poor mother Kanykey.
His bearing and appearance,
Each limb, his very shape,
Had become like his father Manas's.
The people who watched
Seemed to see that man running.
The enemy plainly seemed
To despair of life.
Leaving offspring behind,
Plainly the leopard Manas,
The man, seemed to have come alive.
To the plump, gray-mottled goshawk,
Her heart aching, unable to stand,
For the morning star left by her husband Manas,
With many worries in her heart,
For her foal, the child Kanykey had borne,
Raging and grieving,
With only a spoonful of blood left,
Her flesh reduced to gray lean meat,
Raging, coming straight ahead,
Aktulpar from the palace
His maternal grandfather, Khan Temir,
Led forth and offered as a gift.
Putting a belt about his neck,
Khan Temir stood lamenting,
Pleading with Semetey:
“Oh, Semetey, my foal,
If you wish to go to your father,
Many bear evil thoughts;
Many enemies await an encounter with you.
The Chinese are on your flank,
Guns are before you;
Many enemies stand ready to contend with you.
I taught it speech for the enemy;
Let me give you a companion from the mute beasts.
My foal, orphan Semetey,
